survivors.title: The permission engine keys caps on the MAIN FRAME domain, so a third-party iframe on an approved dApp spends that dApp's caps
survivors.claim: Direct answer to the lens question 'does any of this change what the permission engine sees'. It does NOT — and that is the problem, because what it sees was already frame-blind. `extractDomain(browser, request)` takes only `browser` and `request`, and resolves the domain from `browser->GetMainFrame()->GetURL()` (:5180-5184), falling back to the Referer (:5196-5210). The `frame` parameter IS in scope at the :3979 call site and is deliberately not passed. So a cross-origin iframe or third-party script inside an approved dApp gets `X-Requesting-Domain: <the dApp>`, and rust-wallet/src/permission_service/request_gate.rs:807 short-circuits to Proceed on trust=approved, after which payment caps are keyed on the dApp's row. I am labelling this PRE-EXISTING, not caused by 9b73bd7 — but it is the attribution path into which 9b73bd7 routes a newly widened set of URLs (both spellings of 3321/2121/8080), which is exactly the surface a third-party embedded dApp widget uses.
survivors.why_it_matters: Real money. The per-tx / per-session caps a user grants to a site they trust are inherited by every ad frame, analytics script and embedded widget that site loads. The 'domain trust' boundary is a top-level-document boundary, not an origin boundary.
survivors.how_to_confirm: Approve a domain you control at, say, a $1 per-tx cap. Embed an iframe from a DIFFERENT origin on it that POSTs to http://127.0.0.1:31401/createAction. Read the wallet log for the X-Requesting-Domain value: if it names the parent, not the iframe, this is confirmed. Negative control: repeat with the same iframe at top level and confirm it is instead prompted as an unknown domain.
survivors.refuter_reasoning:
PARTIALLY SURVIVES, HEAVILY NARROWED, SEVERITY CUT.

CITATION VERIFIED CURRENT. extractDomain is at cef-native/src/core/HttpRequestInterceptor.cpp:5173-5215 (main-frame arm 5177-5193, referrer fallback 5195-5211), signature takes only (browser, request), called at :3846 and :3979, and `frame` IS in scope at GetResourceHandler (:3730-3733) unused. request_initiator - the frame-accurate origin - is also in scope one level up at simple_handler.cpp:8041 and unused. request_gate.rs:807 is verbatim `if trust == "approved" { return GateOutcome::Proceed; }`. The HTTP transport is genuinely web-reachable: SimpleHandler::GetResourceRequestHandler (:8171-8194) matches on URL only with no frame/role restriction (the role_ arm at :8071 is an early BYPASS for trusted overlays, not a restriction); isWalletEndpoint (:5103-5160) includes /createAction and /transaction/; AsyncWalletResourceHandler::GetResponseHeaders (:1420-1423) emits Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * so CORS preflight is not a gate; :3599 sets X-Requesting-Domain from the main-frame-derived value and d0ee6db's denylist (:3652-3659) strips the page's own copy. So on the raw-fetch transport the reading holds.

FOUR SUBSTANTIVE REFUTATIONS OF THE FILING AS WRITTEN.

(1) THE HEADLINE IS FALSE ON THE PRIMARY TRANSPORT, AND THE PANELIST NEVER CHECKED IT. The finding asserts a property of "the permission engine" and of the domain-trust boundary generally. The documented dApp bridge is the wallet_call IPC, not a fetch (CLAUDE.md architecture note; simple_handler.cpp:2074-2091). ResolveIpcOrigin (simple_handler.cpp:2008-2029) derives `origin = hodos::OriginFromUrl(frame->GetURL())` FIRST, and walks ancestors ONLY when that is empty (about:blank/data:/blob:), falling back to main frame only after that. OriginFromUrl (PortConfig.h:104-122) returns the authority - the same host:port shape extractDomain produces, so keys are format-compatible. A cross-origin ad iframe on an approved dApp sending wallet_call is therefore attributed to ITS OWN host:port and lands on the unknown-domain prompt/deny path. The stated scenario does not work on the main, and recently-hardened, path. The finding cites only extractDomain and shows no evidence the other transport was examined.

(2) HALF THE "WHY IT MATTERS" IS NOT A DEFECT. A third-party <script src> in the main document IS the dApp's origin under every browser's security model. Attributing it to the dApp is correct universal behaviour, not a boundary violation. Only the cross-origin-subframe half is a real claim; "analytics script" and "third-party script" are void.

(3) THE 9b73bd7 ATTRIBUTION IS VACUOUS. `git show 9b73bd7 -- cef-native/src/handlers/simple_handler.cpp` shows hodos::IsWalletHostPort(url) was ALREADY the first arm of that if before the commit; only the 3321/2121/8080 literals changed. An attacker frame never needed a foreign bridge port - http://127.0.0.1:31301/createAction has always matched, in both host spellings. 9b73bd7 widened the surface for COOPERATING dApps, adding zero attacker reachability. The claim that it "routes a newly widened set of URLs" into this path is unsupported by the diff.

(4) THE :807 GLOSS IS MISLEADING. That short-circuit is the domain-trust STAGE only; its own comment at :804-805 reads "Approved -> fall through to the kind dispatch." Approval does not bypass dispatch_payment. The phrasing invites the reader to think it does.

SEVERITY: HIGH -> MEDIUM. Compound precondition (user has APPROVED a dApp for wallet access, AND that dApp embeds attacker-controlled cross-origin content, AND the attacker uses the raw-fetch transport rather than the frame-correct bridge). Blast radius bounded by the dApp's own row - default $1.00/tx, $10.00/session - with the gold-pill tab indicator firing on every auto-approved spend and an activity-log entry per spend. Not an unbounded silent drain. Pre-existing and outside the range under review, as the panelist concedes.

WHAT ACTUALLY SURVIVES, RESTATED PRECISELY: the two transports disagree about what "the requesting domain" is. The IPC bridge keys on the FRAME's origin; the HTTP interception path keys on the MAIN FRAME's, discarding both `frame` and `request_initiator` that are in scope. That inconsistency is the defensible defect and it is transport-specific, not a property of the permission engine.

LABELLING: correct. The panelist said CODE_READING and it is one. So is my rebuttal - I did not build, run the browser, or drive a subframe fetch end-to-end, and neither did they. Confidence high on the code reading of both paths; moderate on real-world exploitability of the HTTP path, which remains unmeasured by anyone.

refuted.title: The `outputs` decoy also converts /transaction/send's sendMax fail-closed path into a silent full sweep whenever the price cache is empty
refuted.why:
REFUTED as filed. The cited locations are all current and the C++ mechanism is real — I reproduced it independently — but the causal chain is self-contradicting.

MEASUREMENT (mine, independent). Subject: production header cef-native/include/core/PaymentCost.h included by absolute path (I diffed the scratchpad copy the original panelist compiled against — byte-identical); MSVC 14.44.35207 x64, /std:c++17, nlohmann_json 3.12.0 from C:/Users/archb/Dev/vcpkg/installed/x64-windows-static, the version cef-native/build/CMakeCache.txt resolves. Standalone console exe, not the browser. Probe at scratchpad/pc_probe.cpp. Results:
  baseline sendMax                              price=15.00  sats=0 cents=0 priceAvail=0
  DECOY sendMax + outputs:[]                    price=15.00  sats=0 cents=0 priceAvail=1
  DECOY sendMax + outputs:[]  price cache EMPTY price=-1.00  sats=0 cents=0 priceAvail=0   <-- negative control

Row 3 is the refutation. PaymentCost.h:117 is `c.priceAvailable = (bsvPriceUsd > 0);`. The finding's precondition is "whenever the price cache is empty" — but with an empty price cache C++ reports priceAvailable=0, i.e. exactly the fail-closed PriceUnavailable prompt the finding claims is removed. The finding conflated two distinct caches: the C++ BSVPriceCache feeding bsvPriceUsd, and the Rust price_cache feeding the resolve at handlers.rs:9711.

CODE_READING: those two caches cannot diverge in the required direction under any condition the finding names. BSVPriceCache::fetchFromBackend (HttpRequestInterceptor.cpp:480-500) reads ONLY GET /wallet/bsv-price -> handlers.rs:10044 get_bsv_price -> PriceCache::get_price() (price_cache.rs:156-179). Every branch of get_price() returning >0 implies the in-memory cache is Some at that instant (live fetch calls set(); the stale branch reads that same cache). get_stale() (price_cache.rs:198-201) is `cache.as_ref().map(...)` and set() only ever writes Some, so once Rust has a price it never returns to None for the process lifetime; main.rs:706 price_cache.load_persisted() re-seeds it from the V21 bsv_price_cache SQLite row across restarts. So "C++ price >0 while Rust get_cached().or_else(get_stale()) is None" needs the conjunction: wallet process restarted without the browser restarting, AND the persisted row absent (persist never once succeeded), AND all providers down simultaneously. The finding names none of these terms — it names "fresh profile before the first price fetch" and "all providers down", both of which leave C++ with no price either (row 3).

The other two ways resolved can be None are benign or self-limiting: sats == 0 (nothing to sweep), and a balance read error — and dispatch_payment locks the same DB ~15 lines later (request_gate.rs:1120-1130) returning internal_error_envelope("db_mutex_poisoned"), i.e. deny not proceed.

In the ONLY case actually measured (healthy price), the decoy is inert: resolved is Some and request_gate.rs:1111-1113 overwrites satoshis/cents/bsv_price_available with the balance-derived sweep before build_payment_context sees them.

MISLABELLED: filed as evidence kind MEASUREMENT. The measured datum (priceAvail=1 at a healthy price) is real and I reproduced it, but it is the case where the exploit does not fire. The headline claim was never measured and measures the opposite way when you do. The body does self-label the tail CODE_READING, so this is a header/body mismatch rather than fabrication.

Residual (LOW, not REFUTED outright): the sendMax sentinel at PaymentCost.h:67-70 IS bypassable by arm ordering, and the ResolvedAmount override is the only thing holding that path up — a fragile guard worth fixing (test sendMax before the outputs arm; add the decoy body to SendMaxIsNeverPriceAvailable at cef-native/tests/payment_cost_test.cpp:117-124, which today passes only because its fixture has no `outputs` key). Verified reachable in principle: wallet_call is on the 4-name web-page allowlist (simple_handler.cpp:2046-2051), /transaction/ is matched by isWalletEndpoint (HttpRequestInterceptor.cpp:5124), and SendTransactionRequest (handlers.rs:9609-9617) has no deny_unknown_fields so the extra key does not 400. But the reachable consequence is not a silent sweep.

Not this finding, flagged for the referee: my probe rows 5-6 show /wallet/peerpay/send and /wallet/paymail/send with amount_satoshis:100000000 + outputs:[] pricing as sats=0 cents=0 priceAvail=1 at a HEALTHY price, and neither endpoint has any ResolvedAmount override — plain dispatch_payment, header values survive. That variant has no precondition at all. If a separate decoy finding is on the docket, the severity belongs there, not here.

refuted.title: The sendMax balance read excludes backup UTXOs that the sweep can actually spend, so the resolved amount can under-report
refuted.why:
REFUTED as filed. The SQL asymmetry the panelist describes is real, but the state it requires is not produced by any write path in this tree, so the invariant the comment relies on is NOT falsified.

CITATIONS — all current, one materially incomplete:
- `rust-wallet/src/database/output_repo.rs:265-282` `calculate_balance`, backup filter at :276 — CORRECT.
- `output_repo.rs:69-85` `get_spendable_by_user`, `derivation_prefix IS NOT NULL` at :81, `(o.basket_id IS NULL OR b.name = 'default')` at :82 — CORRECT.
- `handlers.rs:9700-9727` sendMax gate; `calculate_balance` called at :9706 — CORRECT. Comment asserting the over-estimate is at :9694-9696.
- `handlers.rs:13046-13047` — this is a COMMENT describing the prefix convention, not a write. They cited the comment and stopped four lines short of the line that refutes them.

THE REFUTATION (CODE_READING): every site that writes `derivation_prefix = '1-wallet-backup'` also writes `basket_id = <'wallet-backup' basket>`, never NULL and never 'default':
- `handlers.rs:13713` `let backup_basket_id = basket_repo.find_or_insert("wallet-backup", 1).ok();` → consumed by the PushDrop insert at :13717-13723 (`Some("1-wallet-backup"), Some("1")`) and the marker insert at :13726-13733.
- `handlers.rs:14291` — same line, feeding the second pair at :14295-14301 and :14305-14312.
Those four are the ONLY writers of that prefix. I enumerated every other write of `derivation_prefix` in the crate: `upsert_received_utxo_with_confirmed` (`output_repo.rs:463-471`) writes NULL for the backup marker index -3 and `"2-receive address"`/`"master"` otherwise; `store_derived_utxo` (`handlers.rs:7008`) uses the hardcoded constant `"2-3241645161d8"` — the peer-supplied token values go into the SUFFIX only, so a hostile PeerPay sender cannot inject the backup prefix; `update_derivation_with_sender` (`output_repo.rs:659`) has two callers, both passing the literal `"1-identity"` (`certificate_handlers.rs:4291`, `:5073`); `main.rs:633` writes `'master'`. `backup.rs:498` excludes the backup prefix from the export, so the restore insert at `backup.rs:1460` can never re-materialize one. No migration backfills `outputs`.

So `get_spendable_by_user`'s basket clause excludes every backup output that actually exists, and the sweep pool never contains one.

MEASUREMENT (synthetic, SQL semantics only — NOT an app measurement, and I did not run the browser or the wallet): I reproduced both queries verbatim against an in-memory SQLite with three rows — a backup output as actually written (basket 'wallet-backup'), the panelist's hypothetical (same row, basket NULL), and ordinary change. Sweep returned rows [2,3]; balance returned 5000. i.e. the divergence appears ONLY for the hypothetical row, and the as-written row is correctly excluded from both. This confirms the mechanism is real and confirms the as-shipped state does not trigger it.

(a) Could this pass with the feature removed? N/A — this is a refutation, not an acceptance test. (b) SUBJECT: the Rust wallet source at HEAD of branch 0.4.0; the SQLite run measured only the two SQL strings, transcribed by hand, not the binary. (c) If the finding were true I would expect at least one `insert_output`/UPDATE writing `'1-wallet-backup'` with a NULL or default basket, or a code path moving such a row into the default basket. I looked at all of them; none exists. (d) My core claim is a CODE_READING; the SQLite run is a measurement of SQL semantics only and I am not dressing it up as more.

RESIDUAL (why INFO and not REFUTED-to-zero): two latent routes to the state the panelist assumed, neither demonstrated and neither claimed by them:
1. `find_or_insert(...).ok()` at :13713/:14291 swallows a SQL error to `None` → basket NULL. Requires a DB error, not a normal path.
2. `relinquish_output` (`handlers.rs:16368`, `remove_from_basket` at :16484) sets `basket_id = NULL` on any outpoint whose basket the caller names correctly. A caller that relinquishes the backup PushDrop from basket 'wallet-backup' WOULD move it into the sweep pool and out of the balance. That is a genuinely interesting, separate question about relinquish vs. the backup token — it is not evidence for this finding, and I am flagging it as a distinct lead rather than smuggling it in as confirmation.

SEVERITY: claimed LOW, corrected to INFO. The "why it matters" is wrong on its own terms — the invariant holds under all current writers — and even the hypothetical harm is bounded: it would only under-price a sweep by the backup token + 546-sat marker, and the effect is bounded further because a spent backup token is a wallet-integrity problem long before it is a permission-gate problem. The c5b link is also loose: c5b is about SUPERSEDED backup phantoms lingering spendable INSIDE the wallet-backup basket, which the basket filter keeps out of the sweep for the same reason.

Confidence: high on the enumeration of write paths (grep was exhaustive over `derivation_prefix` writes and over `INSERT INTO outputs`); medium-high that no runtime path produces an orphaned/NULL basket on a backup row, since I could not inspect a real production DB read-only within this panel's constraints. If someone wants to close the residual cheaply, the defensive fix is one line: add `AND COALESCE(o.derivation_prefix,'') != '1-wallet-backup'` to `get_spendable_by_user` so the two queries agree structurally instead of agreeing by accident of basket assignment.

refuted.title: A bypass of this gate leaves no production trace
refuted.why:
REFUTED on its central claim. My work is CODE_READING throughout — I ran no browser, no wallet, no request. The filer's own CODE_READING label was honest, so no mislabelling.

WHAT I CONFIRMED (the filer's citations are all CURRENT at HEAD):
- rust-wallet/src/main.rs:112 — the refusal is `log::warn!("🛡️ REFUSED {} {} from dApp origin '{}' …")`, and main.rs:117 carries `"error": "permission_table_is_first_party_only"`. Gate body is main.rs:77-124.
- rust-wallet/src/main.rs:203 — `let default_level = if app_dir_name() == "HodosBrowserDev" { "info" } else { "warn" };` Production default IS warn.
- rust-wallet/src/main.rs:1025 — `.wrap(middleware::Logger::new("%a \"%r\" %s %b …"))` with no `.log_level()` override. I checked the pinned dependency (Cargo.toml:36 `actix-web = "=4.11.0"`) against the vendored source: actix-web-4.11.0/src/middleware/logger.rs:106 and :264 default `log_level: Level::Info`, emitted via `log::log!` at :450-452. So `%r` IS suppressed at prod warn. Correct.
- rust-wallet/src/handlers.rs:10135 — `set_domain_permission` logs its success at `log::info!("📋 POST /domain/permissions domain={}")`, also suppressed. Correct.
- No automated test: `permission_table_is_first_party_only` appears at exactly two places — main.rs:117 and development-docs/0.4.0-beta.3/phase-0.5-money-path/PHASE_CONTRACT.md:573. Nothing in rust-wallet/tests/ (17 files) or any `#[cfg(test)]` references `domain_trust_mw` or gate-relevant `X-Requesting-Domain` behavior. Correct.

WHY IT IS STILL REFUTED — the load-bearing claim is false:
The finding asserts "a successful bypass produces exactly the same production log as no request at all" and titles itself "leaves no production trace." Both fail, for two independent reasons.

(1) The C++ browser process logs the request unconditionally in RELEASE builds, BEFORE Rust ever sees it. cef-native/src/core/Logger.cpp:30-55 (`Logger::Log`) has NO level filter whatsoever — it formats the line and writes it to the open file, for every level including DEBUG. `Logger::Initialize` is called unconditionally at cef-native/cef_browser_shell.cpp:4601 in production. Consequently:
  - cef-native/src/handlers/simple_handler.cpp:8189-8192 — any URL matching `hodos::IsWalletHostPort` (PortConfig.h:161-165, which matches both `localhost:31301` and `127.0.0.1:31301`) logs `"🌐 Intercepting wallet request from browser role: " + role_` and hands off to `HttpRequestInterceptor`.
  - cef-native/src/core/HttpRequestInterceptor.cpp:3740 — `LOG_DEBUG_HTTP("🌐 HTTP Request intercepted: " + method + " " + url)`. This is the FULL URL, verbatim, including any percent-encoded path. The filer's specific claim that "%r … is where a percent-encoded path would be visible" is therefore wrong: the encoded path is visible in debug_output.log regardless of the Rust log level.
  - On the IPC route, HttpRequestInterceptor.cpp:2059 logs `origin + " endpoint=" + endpoint`, and :2195 logs origin + trust_level.
This is corroborated by the project's own prior measurement that production accumulates a ~1.58 GB plaintext log of every URL with no rotation — that pathology exists precisely BECAUSE these DEBUG lines are unfiltered in release.

(2) The bypass's entire payload is a WRITE to `domain_permissions`. A persisted row is a stronger and longer-lived trace than a log line: it is durable, queryable, and surfaced in the product's own UI (the right-click "Manage Site Permissions" flow / settings permission list). "Leaves no production trace" is simply not what the code does.

SCOPE ERROR: the finding's argument is sound only if "production log" is silently narrowed to the Rust wallet.log file alone. It never states that narrowing, and the title generalizes past it.

REACHABILITY / THREAT MODEL: I accept the scenario is web-page-reachable in principle (it is contingent on finding 1, which I did not adjudicate), so I am not refuting on reachability.

SEVERITY: MEDIUM is inflated. This finding has zero money impact of its own, is wholly conditional on another finding being real, and is factually wrong on the observability claim that is its entire reason for existing. What survives is a narrower, different item: there is NO regression test for the main.rs:77-124 gate, so a re-break would not be caught by CI. That is real test debt worth a backlog line — INFO — but it should be refiled as a test-coverage item, not as an observability finding, and it must not carry the "no production trace" framing.

CAVEAT, stated honestly (low confidence, forward-looking): the C++ trace I am relying on lives in debug_output.log, which the team's own LOGGING_REVIEW_AND_UPGRADE.md work may level-filter or remove for privacy reasons. If a level filter lands on Logger::Log, that trace disappears and this finding's premise would become true. I did not read that doc's current disposition. Worth one sentence in whatever ticket closes the C++ logging privacy work: "a level filter here also deletes the only production record of page-originated wallet requests — replace it with an explicit warn-level security event before removing the DEBUG lines."

SEPARATE OBSERVATION, offered because it is adjacent and I verified it while checking the filer's audit-trail assumptions (CODE_READING, high confidence): `permission_audit_log` (V20, migrations.rs:1111) appears to be a DEAD write path. `permission_service::audit::build_audit_entry` (audit.rs:72) has no production caller — grep finds it only in its own unit test at audit.rs:163-165 — and `PermissionAuditRepository` is re-exported at database/mod.rs:70 but never constructed outside tests. If that holds, the wallet maintains an audit table it never writes to, which is a genuine observability gap of the kind this filer was reaching for. I flag it as unverified-by-execution and recommend it be filed and checked on its own merits rather than folded into this finding.

refuted.title: 9b73bd7 introduced a page-triggerable HTTPS→HTTP downgrade for arbitrary third-party origins, and a /health hijack, via the unanchored IsWalletHostPort substring
refuted.why:
CITATIONS ARE CURRENT, MECHANISM IS NOT. Every location the panelist cited is accurate: PortConfig.h:161-164 IsWalletHostPort is an unanchored whole-URL substring search; HttpRequestInterceptor.cpp:3773-3777 is the new downgrade block; :5117 is the new /health arm; simple_handler.cpp:8187 admits on the same predicate. I verified all four. The finding still fails.

CLAIM 1 (the HIGH half, https->http downgrade of third-party requests) IS REFUTED AT THE MECHANISM. The downgrade block lives inside HttpRequestInterceptor::GetResourceHandler (function opens at HttpRequestInterceptor.cpp:3730). libcef marks the request READ-ONLY before invoking that callback, so request->SetURL() is a silent no-op in a Release build:
  - libcef/browser/net_service/resource_request_handler_wrapper.cc:762 -> state->pending_request_->SetReadOnly(true);
  - ...then :784-786 -> state->handler_->GetResourceHandler(..., state->pending_request_.get());
  - libcef/common/request_impl.cc:205-207 -> CefRequestImpl::SetURL() begins with CHECK_READONLY_RETURN_VOID();
  - libcef/common/request_impl.cc:168-172 -> that macro is DCHECK(false); return; i.e. a no-op with DCHECKs off.
This matches the CEF contract in cef-binaries/include/cef_resource_request_handler.h:104 ("The |request| object cannot not be modified in this callback"). URL mutation is honored ONLY in OnBeforeResourceLoad (:82-83, "treated as a redirect"), and neither SimpleHandler nor HttpRequestInterceptor implements OnBeforeResourceLoad -- the only two implementations in the tree are in cef-native/include/core/AdblockCache.h:75,136.
Therefore for https://bank.example/px?x=127.0.0.1:31301: isWalletEndpoint(url) is false, so HttpRequestInterceptor.cpp:3898 returns nullptr and the DEFAULT LOADER ISSUES THE ORIGINAL, UNMODIFIED HTTPS REQUEST. The rewrite touches only the local std::string. No cleartext third-party request, no cookie exposure, no mixed-content bypass. The claimed shipped-defect-grade regression cannot occur.

FALLOUT WORTH REPORTING SEPARATELY (not a defect, an inertness): AsyncWalletResourceHandler rebuilds its target as hodos::WalletBaseUrl() + endpoint_ (HttpRequestInterceptor.cpp:3588), and the only downstream consumers of the local url are isSocketIOConnection(url) and a scheme-length-agnostic find("://") endpoint extraction (:3862-3867). The scheme downgrade therefore appears FUNCTIONALLY INERT in both directions -- 9b73bd7's GREEN was almost certainly produced entirely by its defect-3 /health arm. That is the opposite of a HIGH-severity regression and should be raised with the commit author as dead code, not as a security finding.

refuted.title: The gold pill does not fire on the runIpcCallDirect path, so the loopback-origin spend in finding 1 is also invisible to the user's primary safeguard
refuted.why:
CODE_READING throughout (I ran nothing; no browser, no spend). The panelist's label is honest — this is a code reading and they called it one, so no mislabelling.

WHAT SURVIVES (the raw observation is true and the citations are CURRENT):
- `cef-native/src/core/HttpRequestInterceptor.cpp:1917-1957` is exactly `runIpcCallDirect`, and an awk scan of 1917-1960 finds **zero** `OnWalletCallSuccess` calls. Confirmed absent.
- The pill does fire at `:2128` (runIpcEngineCascade silent forward), `:3058`, `:3065`, `:3168`, `:3279`, `:3531`, `:4551`. Confirmed.
- `HandleIpcWalletCall` (`:2165`) routes `IsInternalOrigin(origin)` callers to `runIpcCallDirect` at `:2177-2181`. Confirmed.
- The §4j/R4 quote is accurate (`PHASE_CONTRACT.md:103`).

WHY THE FINDING AS FILED IS REFUTED:

1. **Zero independent remediation — it is finding 1 restated.** The pill is a *post-hoc badge on an auto-approved payment*. In the postulated scenario the payment already crossed with no engine cascade, no gate, no modal, no `X-Requesting-Domain`. Fixing finding 1 (stop classifying a loopback *tab* as wallet-internal) routes that caller into `runIpcEngineCascade`, which fires the pill at `:2128` — this "gap" disappears with no code written against it. A finding that requires no fix of its own, and whose consequence (missing badge) is strictly dominated by its own premise (unauthorized spend), is not a separate MEDIUM. It double-counts.

2. **The framing "the pill does not fire on the runIpcCallDirect path" implies a path-specific omission. It is not.** The HTTP transport does the identical thing: `AsyncWalletResourceHandler::Open` at `:2240-2245` takes the `IsInternalOrigin` bypass and `return true`s **before** the `computePaymentCost` block at `:4581`ff that stashes `preCalculatedCents_`. So an internal-origin caller gets no payment-cost derivation and no pill on *either* transport. "Internal origin ⇒ no pill" is one symmetric architectural consequence of the trust classification, not an IPC-side oversight.

3. **Not a regression, so the CLAUDE.md "must survive every refactor" hook does not apply.** `git log -L 1917,1960` shows the function was born pill-less in `3b3e063` (pre-range, Phase 2.5 bridge commit 3). Nothing in `637e216..HEAD` touched it. No refactor removed the pill from anywhere.

4. **Reachability by a WEB PAGE is not established, and I could not construct it.** For `ResolveIpcOrigin` (`simple_handler.cpp:2008-2031`) to yield a loopback authority, the *calling V8 context* must itself be a document whose authority is `127.0.0.1[:port]` / `localhost[:port]` — `hodos::OriginFromUrl` (`PortConfig.h:104-122`) is scheme-anchored, strips userinfo, and empties out for `data:`/`about:blank`/`blob:`, which then inherit the ancestor and finally the `opaque-origin.invalid` sentinel. `cefMessage` is per-V8-context; a remote attacker page cannot execute script inside a cross-origin loopback frame (SOP), so it cannot borrow that context's `cefMessage`. It can *navigate* an iframe to `http://127.0.0.1:5137/...`, but the document it gets is our own React SPA, not attacker JS. Getting attacker JS at a loopback authority requires either a local HTTP server the attacker controls (= local code execution, out of this threat model per the panel rules) or an XSS in our own :5137 SPA — which is a different, unfiled finding. The panelist inherited reachability from finding 1 rather than proving it.

5. **The "same family as the three farbling harnesses" analogy is inflation.** Those were FALSE GREENS — tests that passed with the feature absent. R4 is a green *with an observed RED run in-session* on the scope it states (`OnWalletCallSuccess fired (79 cents … /transaction/send)` and `(63 cents … /wallet/peerpay/send)`, per `PHASE_CONTRACT.md:103`). §4j's overlay sentence is a scoped statement about the first-party send form and never asserts `runIpcCallDirect` is tab-unreachable, so it is not a claim that was falsified.

6. **"Invisible" is overstated even granting the premise.** `/wallet/activity` (`handlers.rs:12356`) derives the ledger from the transaction/output tables, so any spend down this path still appears in the wallet's activity list. The pill is the primary *real-time* safeguard, not the only record.

Residual worth keeping (low confidence, and it belongs to finding 1, not here): if a failed navigation to `http://localhost:<dead port>` leaves `frame->GetURL()` as the target URL, `ResolveIpcOrigin` would return a loopback authority for that error document — but Chromium error pages are opaque-origin and cross-origin to the parent, so I see no way to run script there. Not asserted as a defect.

Verdict: accurate code reading, correctly labelled, but not an independent defect and not shown reachable by a web page. Downgrade MEDIUM → INFO and fold into finding 1 as a consequence note.

refuted.title: §4k's pairing control is the right control for the transport it covers, but it does not reach the header-free transport — the permission table is still writable without a modal from a loopback page
refuted.why:
REFUTED as a finding. The facts it states are true; the finding it builds out of them is not.

**1. The cited code is current (with drift), and says what they claim — but what it says is not a defect.** CODE_READING. `rust-wallet/src/main.rs`: the header read is at :63-69, the early return is at :72-75 (they cited 69-72), and the §4k gate is at :101-122 (they cited 100-118). Off by 2-4 lines each — verified by `grep -n "" | sed -n '59,125p'`. Structurally their claim holds: the gate is after the `None => return Ok(next.call(req)...)` early return. But they then concede this placement is *correct and deliberate*, and propose no change at their own cited location. There is no alternative: moving the gate above the early return 403s every first-party writer, including the modal-approval write itself. **A finding whose location has no available fix is not a finding about that location.**

I independently re-verified the half of their claim that supports the fix: `HttpRequestInterceptor.cpp:2437-2439` sets `Content-Type` only on `POST /domain/permissions`, and `simple_handler.cpp:5200-5230` (`grant_scoped_permission`) builds its body/URL with no `X-Requesting-Domain`. So "every legitimate writer reaches Rust header-free" checks out.

**2. The title scenario is out of this threat model; the body scenario is borrowed and unverified.** The title says "writable ... from a **loopback page**." A page whose origin is `localhost:*`/`127.0.0.1:*` requires either local code execution or a vulnerable local service — the panel rules exclude exactly that. In production nothing of ours serves HTML on loopback except `:5137`, which `GetResourceRequestHandler` (`simple_handler.cpp:8062-8067`) intercepts and serves from `{app}\frontend` on disk. The *body* then silently swaps in a different, broader scenario ("finding 1 shows a web page can reach Rust with no header") — which the panelist did not verify, and for which they explicitly state their own measurement is null ("both directions ... are consistent with the hole remaining open"). **Zero independent evidence for the load-bearing premise; the title and the body are not the same claim.**

**3. It is wholly derivative, and double-counts one root cause.** If finding 1 stands, this adds no attack surface and no fix — the permission table is a *symptom*, and far from the worst one: header-free means `createAction` spends ungated, `getPublicKey` reveals identity silently, and the wallet-backup/mnemonic surface becomes internal-trusted. If finding 1 falls, this finding is empty. Either way the fix belongs at the derivation, not at main.rs.

**4. Severity is inconsistent in both directions.** MEDIUM is wrong for a total trust escalation (that is CRITICAL, and belongs to finding 1) and wrong for a docs-scoping note (INFO). Corrected to INFO: the only thing here that survives is the narrow, correct observation that the ✅ CLOSED row should read "closed *for the header-carrying transport*."

**5. I checked the premise myself and could not confirm it from the transports this range touches — but I did find the concrete candidate, and it is not where they put it.** CODE_READING, confidence medium. The IPC transport is closed: `ResolveIpcOrigin` (`simple_handler.cpp:2008-2030`) is scheme-anchored via `hodos::OriginFromUrl` (`PortConfig.h:104-125`, strips userinfo through the last `@`), walks the ancestor chain for `about:blank`/`data:`/`blob:`, and falls closed to `opaque-origin.invalid` — which `IsInternalOrigin` (`HttpRequestInterceptor.cpp:1016-1024`) rejects, so the header gets stamped and §4k fires. **But the HTTP-interception transport still uses the pre-C1 derivation: `HttpRequestInterceptor::extractDomain` at `HttpRequestInterceptor.cpp:5173-5215`** — unanchored `find("://")`, no userinfo strip, reads `browser->GetMainFrame()` rather than the requesting frame, and returns `""` when the main frame URL has no `://`. `""` → `IsInternalOrigin("")==true` → the bypass at :2240 → and the stamp at :3598-3600 is guarded by `if (!requestDomain_.empty())`, so the call reaches Rust header-free. `git merge-base --is-ancestor cc6cf19 637e216` confirms this predates the range and was **not** swept by C1's "one spelling" rule. The referrer fallback at :5196-5211 is defeatable with `referrerPolicy:'no-referrer'`. I did **not** measure whether a page can actually drive it — that turns on CORS preflight against the handler's `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` at :1420-1422 and on whether Rust answers `OPTIONS` 2xx once the interceptor strips `origin` (:3651). Phase 2.5's own rationale (the IPC bridge exists *because* CSP/CORS blocked renderer fetches to the wallet) argues against reachability.

That belongs as its own finding against the derivation, cited at `HttpRequestInterceptor.cpp:5173`. It does not belong as a scope dispute against §4k, which is correctly built and correctly placed.

refuted.title: The C++ proxy stamps Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * on every wallet response, so Rust's CORS allowlist and block_on_origin_mismatch do not apply to page traffic
refuted.why:
REFUTED on mechanism, on path taxonomy, on security delta, and on range. Citations are current (ACAO * at HttpRequestInterceptor.cpp:1420; kTrustHeaderExact with "origin" at :3650-3656, strip loop :3659-3677; main.rs allowlist :970-999 with block_on_origin_mismatch at :998), but the causal story is wrong.

(1) MECHANISM WRONG, contradicted by an in-tree MEASUREMENT. The claim "origin is stripped so actix-cors sees a header-less request and block_on_origin_mismatch never engages" is false for the POST arm. main.rs:974-988 and development-docs/0.4.0-beta.3/phase-0.5-money-path/ADVERSARIAL_PANEL_2026-08-19.md:105 record that Chromium OVERWRITES Origin on the re-issued POST with request_initiator->Serialize(), and CEF sets request_initiator from the TARGET url, so actix receives Origin: http://127.0.0.1:31301 no matter what the denylist strips. block_on_origin_mismatch DOES engage; it passes only because d0ee6db deliberately allowlisted that origin. PHASE_CONTRACT.md:102 records the RED: remove the two allowlist lines and the live dApp POST comes back carrying a CORS error body. The "origin" denylist entry is defence-in-depth against a page overwriting the header, not the cause of anything.

(2) PATH TAXONOMY INVERTED. The finding contrasts "this transport" with "the DIRECT-fetch path". AsyncWalletResourceHandler IS the direct-fetch path: simple_handler.cpp:8187 routes every wallet-host/port URL from a content-role browser into HttpRequestInterceptor, and the trusted-overlay bypass at :8072 is limited to roles wallet/wallet_panel/settings/backup, which no web page can inhabit. There is no second page-reachable transport being contrasted.

(3) NO SECURITY DELTA. The boundary on that transport is X-Requesting-Domain, stamped by C++ at HttpRequestInterceptor.cpp:3598-3600 from extractDomain() (:5173) BEFORE the page-header merge, and unforgeable because "x-requesting-domain" is in the denylist at :3652. domain_trust_mw (main.rs:59-140) runs ahead of every route and is default-gated for external origins (approved -> proceed, blocked -> 403, unknown -> 202 modal). ACAO:* only lets a page read a reply it was already permitted to receive; removing it would break @bsv/sdk WalletClient and gain nothing, since a blocked read is not a blocked write (the project's own P0.5-C1 rationale). Nothing is exposed that the window.hodosBrowser IPC bridge does not equally expose under the same Rust gate. The filer concedes "This is by design" — which is the correct read.

(4) OUT OF RANGE. ACAO:* dates from 1fa686f (2026-04-21); .allowed_origin("http://127.0.0.1") / ("http://localhost") from 63cda01f (2026-04-17). git log 637e216..HEAD -S on both constructs returns empty. 9b73bd7 did not meaningfully enlarge the set: /health is scoped to IsWalletHostPort and the two foreign bridge ports land on the same gated path.

(5) PORT-80 HALF OUT OF THREAT MODEL AND MISATTRIBUTED. actix-cors does exact Origin string comparison so http://127.0.0.1 matches port 80 only — correct — but exploiting it requires already serving a page from the victim's own loopback port 80, i.e. local code execution. And such a page's fetch to a listed wallet route is intercepted like any other and never reaches actix-cors, so that allowlist entry is not the control governing it.

LABEL: correctly labelled CODE_READING; I did not run anything either, so my counter-analysis is also a CODE_READING, resting on two prior recorded measurements I did not reproduce.

WHAT SURVIVES (INFO): the single true, non-security kernel is that on the intercepted transport the discriminator is X-Requesting-Domain rather than Rust's origin allowlist — already documented at main.rs:44-58. Worth a doc line, not MEDIUM. The "two mental models, only one true" framing is wrong: both are true, each on its own path, and the intercepted path's boundary is the stronger of the two.

ADJACENT, NOT THIS FINDING, LOW CONFIDENCE, NOT RUN: isWalletEndpoint (:5103-5159) is a fixed route table, so a page fetch to a wallet-port path OUTSIDE that table returns nullptr and goes uninterrupted to Rust with NO X-Requesting-Domain, which domain_trust_mw treats as first-party internal. On that residual path actix-cors is the only boundary, which makes the port-less loopback entries load-bearing rather than decorative. That inverts the filed finding rather than supporting it and deserves its own ticket.

negative_results: /health scoping HOLDS for the threat the commit names. I tried to hijack an ordinary site's /health: reaching isWalletEndpoint at all requires the same host:port predicate at simple_handler.cpp:8187, so a normal https://site.com/health is never routed to the interceptor. The only way in is for the page itself to embed the host:port substring in its own URL, which buys the attacker nothing it did not already have (it can call /health directly). The 'must stay host-qualified' comment is correct.

The C2 default-deny IPC gate is genuinely default-deny and I could not get around it from an external origin. It runs at the top of OnProcessMessageReceived (simple_handler.cpp:2067) before any arm dispatches, source_process is irrelevant, and every one of the ~40 arms below it — including send_transaction, peerpay_send, paymail_send and sign_transaction — is refused. ResolveIpcOrigin's cascade (frame -> ancestors -> main frame -> opaque-origin.invalid) has no path that returns an empty string, so the IsInternalOrigin("")==true trap that still bites the HTTP path cannot be reached on the IPC path. Adding a new arm fails closed.

The page-supplied trust-header strip (d0ee6db) resists the bypasses I tried. It lower-cases the name before comparing (HttpRequestInterceptor.cpp:3667-3670), so casing does not evade it; x-payment-* is a prefix strip while x-bsv-price-available is an exact strip, which is the correct split given x-bsv-* is deliberately forwarded; and x-cert-approved-fields and origin are both covered. On the IPC transport the question does not arise at all — runIpcCallDirect and runIpcEngineCascade build their header maps from scratch and never merge page headers.

Allowlisting http://127.0.0.1:31301 / :31401 in the Rust CORS config is safe as claimed. Origin is a forbidden header name for page JS on the fetch path, and on the wallet_call IPC path the page cannot set headers at all. I found no route by which page-controlled bytes become the Origin value.

The X-User-Approved replay path resists forgery. consume_and_verify is single-use, body-sha256-bound and expiring (request_gate.rs:1041-1080), approval ids are minted server-side, and the replay deliberately does not require X-Payment-* headers only because the cents/browser_id come from the stored approval rather than the wire. I could not construct a replay that moves a different amount than the one approved.

Windows is contained against the wallet_call endpoint-injection host swap. ParseUrl splits hostPort at the FIRST ':' and then requires digits-only, <=5 chars, 1..65535, so `@evil.com/x`, `.evil.com/x` and `99999999999` all fail closed. The 491ab15 guard does more than the crash fix it advertises. (macOS is the exception — see the finding.)

The BRC-121 402 chain is gated end to end. TryHandleBrc121_402 requires a non-empty payee host, requires wallet existence, fires domain_approval for any non-approved payee, and then forwards to /wallet/pay402 with X-Requesting-Domain + the X-Payment-* set so Rust's dispatch_payment renders the real decision (HttpRequestInterceptor.cpp:4661-4820). A page cannot make itself the payee of someone else's approved domain, and the sats/pubkey shape checks reject junk 402 headers. I found no ungated arm here.

The resume-after-modal path uses the C++-derived origin, not a page-supplied one: ModalContext is built from `origin`/`requestDomain_` at the point of the 202, and the page only supplies the correlation requestId (resume.originalIpcRequestId). This is a code reading, not a measurement — I did not exercise an approve/deny round trip.

OriginFromUrl (PortConfig.h:104-122) resisted every URL-shape attack I tried on paper: uppercase scheme (`HTTP://`) fails the rfind and returns empty -> cascade -> opaque sentinel (fails closed); userinfo `http://127.0.0.1:5137@evil.com/` correctly yields `evil.com` via the rfind('@') strip at :117-119; trailing dot `localhost.:5137` fails AuthorityHasHost's terminator check (:129-133); IPv6 `[::1]:5137` is not equal to either internal literal so it fails closed; backslash authorities are normalised to '/' by Chromium before GetURL returns the spec. The specific prior-panel exploit `data:text/html,a://127.0.0.1:5137/` now returns empty at step 1, which is what lets the cascade and the opaque-origin.invalid sentinel actually run. The C1 derivation itself is, as far as I can tell, correct.

The `hodos://` prefix arm kept in IsInternalFrontendUrl (PortConfig.h:137) is unreachable as written: I grepped for AddCustomScheme / OnRegisterCustomSchemes across cef-native and found none, and the only producer is NavigationHandler.cpp:27-31 which rewrites the string to http://127.0.0.1:5137/ before navigation. Chromium will not commit a document on an unregistered scheme, so no frame can carry it. The self-flagged inconsistency is real but not exploitable today.

LocalFileResourceRequestHandler (LocalFileResourceHandler.h:42-82) held up: literal `..` is rejected, drive-letter and rooted paths are rejected, and percent-encoded dot segments (%2e%2e) are resolved by Chromium's URL canonicaliser before the spec reaches ExtractPath. I could not find a way to serve an attacker-chosen file from the privileged 127.0.0.1:5137 origin, which would have been a clean escalation to the internal origin.

I hypothesised that service-worker-originated fetches would reach GetResourceRequestHandler with browser==NULL, making extractDomain return "" and IsInternalOrigin("") true — a total header-free bypass from any https site. REFUTED: we register no CefRequestContextHandler anywhere in cef-native (only SimpleHandler::GetResourceRequestHandler exists, simple_handler.cpp:8035), so browserless requests never reach the interceptor. They go to the real network stack where Rust's CORS with block_on_origin_mismatch(true) applies.

Header-injection forgery of the domain is closed on both ends: the C++ denylist strips page-supplied origin / x-requesting-domain / x-user-approved / x-browser-id / x-bsv-price-available / x-cert-approved-fields plus the x-payment-* prefix (HttpRequestInterceptor.cpp:3652-3684), and Rust's domain_trust_mw filters an empty X-Requesting-Domain rather than treating it as a present-but-blank external domain (main.rs:65-70). I could not construct a page-supplied header that reaches actix as a trust signal.

The 491ab15 port guard (SyncHttpClient.cpp:43-75) incidentally closes an SSRF I went looking for: a page-supplied wallet_call endpoint of `@evil.com/x` produces port text `31401@evil.com`, which now fails the digits-only check and returns false rather than reaching WinHttpConnect. The endpoint string remains otherwise unvalidated, as the commit says.

Top-level data: documents do NOT forge an internal IPC origin: ResolveIpcOrigin returns opaque-origin.invalid for them (simple_handler.cpp:2028-2030) and the wallet_call arm logs the fail-closed warning at :2143-2148. Only the HTTP path's extractDomain would mis-parse such a URL, which is finding 2.

DEFAULT-DENY IPC GATE vs every first-party overlay: NOT BROKEN.
